content_voiceover: This slide sets the stage for discussing antithrombin by first laying out the full coagulation cascade in enzyme complex form. On the left, the extrinsic tenase complex, made of factor VIIa, tissue factor, an anionic membrane surface, and calcium, activates factor X. The intrinsic tenase complex, built from factor IXa and factor VIIIa on a membrane surface, also activates factor X, amplifying the signal. Activated factor X then joins factor Va to form the prothrombinase complex, which converts factor II, prothrombin, into thrombin, labeled FIIa. Thrombin has two jobs shown here: it cleaves fibrinogen into crosslinked fibrin, and it activates platelets, which in turn activate factor XI into FXIa, feeding back to generate more factor IXa. This entire diagram represents unchecked coagulation; the next slide overlays the inhibitor that reins it in.
keypoints: Extrinsic and intrinsic tenase complexes activate factor X
Prothrombinase complex converts prothrombin to thrombin
Thrombin generates fibrin and amplifies its own production via factor XI
This cascade diagram is the baseline for showing antithrombin's targets
keypoint_voiceover: This diagram lays out the full amplification loop of coagulation, from tenase complexes generating factor Xa, to prothrombinase generating thrombin, to thrombin driving fibrin formation and feeding back through factor XI. Keep this map in mind because the next slide shows exactly where antithrombin intervenes.
